raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the mortality benefit of ICD therapy while avoiding transvenous leads, venous access, endocardial hardware, pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, tricuspid-valve interaction, and systemic device infection. The concept was validated in feasibility work showing reliable sensing and defibrillation using a left lateral generator and parasternal electrode, albeit with higher defibrillation energy than transvenous systems [1]. Subsequent single-center and multicenter experiences confirmed high induced ventricular fibrillation conversion rates and established the practical implant workflow, including screening for acceptable QRS/T-wave morphology and the importance of pocket and lead positioning [2], [3], [4], [5], [6].

Early real-world registries were pivotal. The EFFORTLESS registry showed acceptable short-term complication-free survival and effective treatment of spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, but also highlighted inappropriate shocks, mainly from oversensing [7]. A pooled analysis of the IDE and EFFORTLESS cohorts found high overall conversion of spontaneous VT/VF episodes and no endovascular lead failures, supporting the biologic premise that extravascular defibrillation could reduce lead-related morbidity [8]. Midterm and long-term EFFORTLESS analyses confirmed durability of the platform, with late complications and infections relatively uncommon, although inappropriate shocks remained clinically important [9], [10]. The U.S. Post-Approval Study extended these findings to a broader cohort with more heart failure, diabetes, renal disease, and community implanting centers; perioperative success was high and 1-year shock efficacy remained favorable [11], [12].

Patient selection is central. The S-ICD is best suited to patients who need defibrillation but not chronic bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP). It is particularly attractive in younger patients, those with inherited arrhythmia syndromes, limited venous access, prior device infection, hemodialysis, congenital heart disease, or high anticipated lifetime lead burden. Conversely, monomorphic VT likely to be ATP-terminable, advanced conduction disease, symptomatic bradycardia, and current or likely near-term CRT needs favor a transvenous or alternative extravascular system. The UNTOUCHED study specifically addressed primary-prevention patients with reduced ejection fraction and contemporary programming; it reported a low inappropriate-shock rate, supporting S-ICD use beyond highly selected young channelopathy cohorts [13].

Randomized evidence has clarified trade-offs. In PRAETORIAN, among patients with an ICD indication but no pacing indication, S-ICD therapy was noninferior to transvenous ICD therapy for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [14]. The ATLAS trial, focused on patients at higher risk for lead complications, showed fewer perioperative lead-related complications with S-ICD implantation [15]. Propensity-matched observational comparisons similarly suggested fewer lead complications and systemic infections but different shock profiles [16]. A PRAETORIAN secondary analysis emphasized this pattern: transvenous systems incur more lead-related complications, whereas S-ICDs require meticulous sensing management and may have more pocket-related or sensing-related events [17].

Inappropriate shocks are the dominant modifiable limitation. Early causes included T-wave oversensing, low R-wave amplitude, myopotentials, supraventricular tachycardia, air entrapment, and suboptimal vector choice. The SMART Pass high-pass filter substantially reduced oversensing-mediated shocks without impairing appropriate therapy [18]. Contemporary analyses show that inappropriate shocks are less frequent with improved screening, dual-zone programming, higher detection thresholds, exercise or posture assessment in selected patients, and routine postimplant vector optimization [19]. The PRAETORIAN score offers a chest-radiograph-based assessment of generator and coil position and predicts elevated defibrillation thresholds, reinforcing that implantation technique is not merely cosmetic but therapeutic [20].

Defibrillation testing remains debated. Unlike contemporary transvenous ICD implantation, in which routine testing has been largely abandoned, S-ICD testing historically confirmed sensing and shock vector adequacy. Observational data and ongoing randomized evidence increasingly support selective rather than universal testing when implant position is optimal and patient risk is high for anesthesia or induction [21]. Programming lessons from transvenous ICD trials—higher rate cutoffs and longer detection—have been incorporated into S-ICD practice and help reduce unnecessary therapy [22], [23]. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses generally conclude that S-ICD and transvenous ICDs provide similar protection from sudden death in appropriately selected patients, with distinct complication phenotypes rather than uniform superiority of one system [24], [25].

Special populations remain important. Pediatric and congenital heart disease experience supports S-ICD use when venous anatomy, growth, or lifetime lead risk is problematic, though generator size, body habitus, and sensing vectors can be challenging [26], [27]. The rationale is strengthened by long-term transvenous lead failure data and pediatric ICD complication registries [28], [29]. Current reviews therefore frame the S-ICD as an established alternative—not a niche device—for patients without pacing indications, while acknowledging future competition from leadless pacing–S-ICD communication and extravascular ICD systems capable of ATP [30]. Overall, the S-ICD has shifted ICD decision-making from “can a lead be placed?” to “what lifetime hardware risk is acceptable?”; optimal outcomes require careful patient selection, ECG screening, precise implantation, contemporary programming, and shared decision-making.
